text: Last lesson covered passive recon's raw sources — WHOIS, DNS, Certificate Transparency. This lesson turns those into a real OSINT methodology, using the tools and search discipline that actual engagements rely on: Shodan, theHarvester, structured Google dorking, and social media footprinting, every one of them still staying on the passive side of the line.

Shodan already scanned the internet, so searching its index for an organization's open ports and exposed services is querying someone else's pre-existing data, not probing the target yourself. theHarvester automates the rest — one command queries dozens of public sources at once and returns deduplicated emails, subdomains, and employee names. Google dorking becomes a repeatable checklist rather than a lucky guess. And social media footprinting, done right, maps org structure and job titles within whatever the signed scope actually authorizes.

A Shodan query like org colon quote Target Company quote port colon 22,3389 surfaces every SSH and RDP service Shodan has already observed exposed for that organization. theHarvester dash d target-company.com dash b all hits every supported source in one pass — search engines, PGP key servers, CT logs, Shodan itself — and hands you back a clean list ready to feed into the attack surface map you'll build in Lesson 8.

Run these as a standing checklist against every in-scope domain: site colon target-company.com filetype colon pdf for exposed documents carrying useful metadata, inurl colon admin for crawled administrative interfaces, and intitle colon quote index of quote for open directory listings nobody meant to leave public. Each operator answers a different question — don't treat dorking as one lucky search.

LinkedIn is a legitimate OSINT source for org charts and job titles, but the discipline that matters is scope: your authorization names specific employees or roles, not "anyone public," so footprinting someone's personal accounts or family beyond that list is a violation even though the data is public. Document every source for every finding. Next lesson, we cross the line from passive to active — the first time a packet actually reaches the target.
